newsitem.title: UK: Record lows for UK PPI, but will it feed through?.
newsitem.headline: Record lows for UK PPI, but will it feed through?.

text.p: Pipeline British inflation set fresh record lows in January but the key question remains whether this will drag high street prices lower.
On balance, economists say retail prices will subside but that may be more to do with signs of slowing consumer spending rather than the continued demise of producer price inflation pressures.
"These figures are uniformly weak," said Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc. "But the key is whether declines in PPI will have a knock-on effect at the retail level."

Uglow said retail prices would in the end by dragged lower but he noted that producer prices have been subdued or falling for more than a year but for many months retail price inflation stuck above three percent year-on-year.
Monday's data showed output prices, those leaving the factory gate, rose at just 1.5 percent year-on-year in January, the lowest rate of increase since October 1986.
Core output prices, excluding food, drink, tobacco and petroleum, rose 0.6 percent on a year earlier -- the lowest inflation rate in 30 years.
Whether retail price inflation slows in tandem or not, Monday's figures will certainly help Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke ward off pressure to increase interest rates anytime soon.
He has insisted on leaving 6.0 percent base rates on hold since last October despite increasing pressure from Bank of England governor Eddie George.
"Mr Clarke may be forgiven a wry smile," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "His judgement, after all, appears more in tune with recent economic data."
Retail price figures for January are due on Thursday. Underlying inflation is forecast to edge down to an annual 3.0 percent, from 3.1 in December.

But more important for the interest rate argument will be the following week's retail sales data. High street sales actually fell 0.8 percent in December, calling into question ideas of a consumer boom.

Analysts said December's sales should always be viewed in conjunction with January's. But evidence from the Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey suggests there was no surge in spending last month either.
"The CBI evidence was relatively weak," Uglow said. "We expected a reported balance of 50 or more."
Some 53 percent of UK retailers surveyed said sales rose in January while 17 percent said sales dropped -- a positive balance of 36 percent.
But given that balance fell from 48 percent in November, to 33 in December, that hardly represented a dramatic turnaround.

One thing is certain though. However the conflicting pressures on high street prices are resolved, there is no upward pressure from the producer level. That, in part, is due to the pound's meteoric rise over the past seven months.

Seasonally adjusted input prices fell a staggering 6.2 percent year-on-year in January. "That confirms the strength of the pound continues to place heavy downward pressure on industry costs," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

But do not expect that to deflect the Bank of England in its crusade for higher interest rates. The Bank releases its quarterly inflation report on Wednesday and is expected to reassert its view that a strong currency is no substitute for tighter monetary policy.
Unemployment figures, due on Wednesday, will also stir the inflation pot this week.
"The big risk to UK inflation is the labour market and wages," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economist at BankAmerica.

He said there was a significant risk that rapidly falling unemployment will force up wages. "If that happens, it will be virtually impossible to keep inflation in check without a rate hike. This makes Wednesday's labour market report almost more important than the RPIs themselves."
